items.stem: Which statement about evaporation is correct?
options: It releases energy to the surroundings.
It takes place only at the surface of a liquid and at temperatures below the boiling point.
It takes place throughout the liquid at the boiling point.
items.answer: It takes place only at the surface of a liquid and at temperatures below the boiling point.
items.markingKey: Evaporation: surface only, any temperature; boiling: throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

items.stem: State what is meant by a reversible reaction.
items.answer: a reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants

items.stem: Tariq writes the equation for "lithium + water → lithium hydroxide + hydrogen" as Li + H₂O → LiOH + H₂. Explain why the equation is not acceptable and write it correctly with state symbols.
items.answer: It is not balanced: the numbers of atoms of each element are not equal on both sides. Correct: 2Li(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2LiOH(aq) + H₂(g).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: not balanced; 1 mark: correct balanced equation [2]

items.stem: A student's titres are (cm³): rough 32.30, 31.15, 31.10, 31.05. What is the mean of the concordant titres?
items.markingKey: Concordant: 31.15, 31.10, 31.05 → mean 31.10 cm³

items.stem: Explain why ethanol dissolves in water but the solution does not conduct electricity.
items.answer: Ethanol is made of neutral molecules; no ions form when it dissolves, so there are no mobile charged particles.

items.stem: A steel tap is to be electroplated with nickel. Name the anode, the cathode and a suitable electrolyte.
items.answer: anode: nickel; cathode: steel tap; electrolyte: aqueous nickel(II) sulfate
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of each other?
items.answer: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C
items.markingKey: Same proton number (6), different mass numbers.

items.stem: Which oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid but not with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
items.answer: calcium oxide
items.markingKey: Basic oxide.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the sum of the oxidation numbers in the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, is −2. (b) Explain, using oxidation numbers, why 2Fe²⁺ + Cl₂ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2Cl⁻ is a redox reaction.
items.answer: (a) The sum of oxidation numbers in an ion equals the charge on the ion: S (+6) + 4 × O (−2) = −2. (b) Fe increases from +2 to +3 (oxidised); Cl decreases from 0 to −1 (reduced).

items.stem: Ana varies the conditions for the reaction of iron with hydrochloric acid, keeping the mass of solid and volume of acid the same. experiment 1: filings, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 25 °C; experiment 2: filings, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 45 °C; experiment 3: powder, 0.250 mol/dm³ acid, 45 °C. Which experiment has the fastest initial rate?
items.answer: experiment 3
items.markingKey: Experiment 3 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: When methane burns in a Bunsen burner, the temperature of the mixture rises. Explain this observation in terms of energy transfer and state the sign of ΔH.
items.answer: The reaction is exothermic: thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings, so their temperature rises. ΔH is negative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: classification; 1 mark: direction of energy transfer; 1 mark: sign of ΔH [3]

items.stem: Sipho traps carbon dioxide in a gas syringe at constant pressure and measures its volume at different temperatures: 10 °C: 20.0 cm³, 35 °C: 21.8 cm³, 60 °C: 23.5 cm³, 85 °C: ? cm³, 110 °C: 27.1 cm³. Describe the relationship between temperature and volume shown by the data.
items.answer: As the temperature increases the volume increases (by equal amounts for equal temperature rises).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: volume increases with temperature; 1 mark: steady / linear [2]

items.stem: For the water–gas shift reaction, CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂, ΔH = −41 kJ/mol, what is the effect of the following change: decrease pressure?
options: The position of equilibrium does not change.
The position of equilibrium shifts to the left.
The position of equilibrium shifts to the right.
items.answer: The position of equilibrium does not change.
items.markingKey: There are equal numbers of moles of gas on each side (2 and 2), so pressure has no effect on the position of equilibrium.

items.stem: In the reaction AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq), which ions are spectator ions?
items.answer: Na⁺ and NO₃⁻
items.markingKey: Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ form the precipitate; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ stay in solution.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student obtains a percentage yield of 108% for a dried precipitate. Suggest a reason for this. (b) Explain why a reversible reaction cannot have a 100% yield.
items.answer: (a) The product was not completely dry (still contained water) or was contaminated with another substance. (b) The products re-form the reactants, so at equilibrium not all reactants have been converted to products.

items.stem: Three solids are tested. A: m.p. 1710 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; B: m.p. 55 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; C: m.p. −114 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify which solid(s) have a giant covalent structure and explain your choice.
items.answer: A: A is giant covalent; B is simple molecular; C is simple molecular
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A; 1 mark: very high m.p. (many strong covalent bonds); 1 mark: does not conduct (or graphite exception) / rules out others [3]

items.stem: The government of a country is deciding whether to build hydrogen filling stations in Kuala Lumpur. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells compared with petrol or diesel engines.
items.answer: Advantage: there are fewer moving parts, so less maintenance and quieter running. Disadvantage: hydrogen is flammable/explosive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: advantage explained; 1 mark: disadvantage explained [2]

items.stem: For each element, write the electronic configuration and state its group and period: lithium (proton number 3), neon (proton number 10), argon (proton number 18).
items.answer: lithium: 2,1, Group I, Period 2; neon: 2,8, Group VIII, Period 2; argon: 2,8,8, Group VIII, Period 3
items.markingKey: lithium: 2,1, Group I, Period 2; neon: 2,8, Group VIII, Period 2; argon: 2,8,8, Group VIII, Period 3. 1 mark per element (configuration with group and period) [3]

items.stem: Which colour does universal indicator turn in a solution of pH 1?
items.answer: red
items.markingKey: Strong acids give red with universal indicator.

items.stem: In the reaction Zn(s) + Pb²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Pb(s), explain which species is the oxidising agent and which is the reducing agent.
items.answer: Pb²⁺ is the oxidising agent: it gains electrons (Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb) and is reduced. Zn is the reducing agent: it loses electrons (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and is oxidised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: oxidising agent with reason; 1 mark: reducing agent with reason [2]

items.stem: Grace measures the time for magnesium to react with acid at different temperatures: 30 °C: 200 s, 40 °C: 100 s, 50 °C: 50 s, 60 °C: 26 s. Describe the trend and explain it using collision theory.
items.answer: As temperature increases the time decreases, so the rate increases (roughly doubling every 10 °C): particles move faster, collide more often, and more collisions have energy ≥ Ea.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: faster at higher temperature; 1 mark: more frequent and more energetic collisions [2]

items.stem: For the reaction 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O, list the bonds broken and the bonds made, and explain how these determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: Broken: 2 × C–C, 12 × C–H, 7 × O=O. Made: 8 × C=O, 12 × O–H. If more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise endothermic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bonds broken; 1 mark: bonds made; 1 mark: comparison rule [3]

items.stem: Daniel places cotton wool soaked in concentrated aqueous ammonia at one end of a 50 cm glass tube and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid at the other end, then seals both ends. After a few minutes a white ring of ammonium chloride forms inside the tube. (a) Calculate the relative molecular masses of ammonia and hydrogen chloride. (b) Explain why the tube is sealed at both ends.
items.answer: (a) NH₃ = 17; HCl = 36.5 (b) To stop the gases escaping (and to stop air currents/draughts affecting the movement).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: The table shows the percentage of ammonia at equilibrium under different conditions. 200 °C: 10 atm 50.7%, 50 atm 74.0%, 100 atm 81.5%, 200 atm 89.0%; 300 °C: 10 atm 14.7%, 50 atm 39.5%, 100 atm 52.5%, 200 atm 66.7%; 500 °C: 10 atm 1.2%, 50 atm 5.6%, 100 atm 10.6%, 200 atm 18.3%. State the percentage yield at 500 °C and 200 atm, and describe the effects of temperature and pressure on the yield.
items.answer: 18.3%. Yield increases as pressure increases and decreases as temperature increases.
items.markingKey: 18.3% [1]; higher pressure → higher yield [1]; higher temperature → lower yield [1]

items.stem: Phosphorus has a valency of 3 and chlorine a valency of 1. Deduce the formula of the compound they form and explain your reasoning.
items.answer: PCl₃
items.markingKey: Combining powers must match: PCl₃ (phosphorus trichloride) [2]

items.stem: 0.100 mol of ammonium chloride is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
items.answer: 0.400 mol/dm³

items.stem: The melting point of calcium chloride, CaCl₂, is 772 °C and that of potassium bromide, KBr, is 734 °C. Explain why both melting points are high, and suggest why calcium chloride has the higher melting point.
items.answer: Both are giant ionic lattices with many strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions that need a lot of energy to overcome. Calcium chloride has ions with larger charges (and/or smaller ions), so the attraction between them is stronger.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: giant ionic lattice; 1 mark: strong electrostatic attraction needs much energy; 1 mark: comparison (charge / size of ions) [3]

items.stem: Felix electrolyses dilute sulfuric acid using graphite electrodes. List the ions present in the solution and predict the product at each electrode, explaining your predictions.
items.answer: Ions: H⁺, SO₄²⁻, OH⁻. Cathode: hydrogen – the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead. Anode: oxygen – there are no halide ions, so OH⁻ ions are discharged to give oxygen.
items.markingKey: ions H⁺, SO₄²⁻, OH⁻ [1]; cathode hydrogen with reason [1]; anode oxygen with reason [1]

items.stem: Classify each of these as an element, a compound or a mixture: glucose, sulfur, mercury, air.
items.answer: glucose: compound; sulfur: element; mercury: element; air: mixture
items.markingKey: glucose: compound; sulfur: element; mercury: element; air: mixture. All 4 correct [2]; 3 or 2 correct [1] total [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid but magnesium does. (b) Explain how the name of the salt formed in an acid reaction depends on the acid used.
items.answer: (a) Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from the acid; magnesium is above hydrogen. (b) The acid provides the anion: hydrochloric acid → chlorides, sulfuric acid → sulfates, nitric acid → nitrates; the metal or base provides the cation.

items.stem: 116 cm³ of CO₂ is produced in the first 40 s when marble chips reacts with hydrochloric acid. Calculate the average rate in cm³/s and in cm³/min.
items.answer: 2.90 cm³/s; 174 cm³/min

items.stem: Samuel writes in a revision note: "Liquid particles stop moving when the liquid is poured into a container." Identify the error and give the correct statement.
items.answer: Liquid particles are always moving randomly and sliding past each other.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: error identified; 1 mark: correct particle explanation [2]

items.stem: Calculate the percentage by mass of C in carbon dioxide, CO₂. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16) Hence calculate the mass of C in 500 g of CO₂.

Nadia heats calcium (proton number 20) in oxygen (proton number 8). A white solid, calcium oxide, is formed. (a) Describe the dot-and-cross diagram of the compound, showing outer shells only. (b) Deduce the formula of the compound. (c) Name the type of force holding the ions together and describe the structure of the solid.
items.answer: (a) 1 Ca²⁺ ion(s) with empty/full outer shell and 1 O²⁻ ion(s) each with 8 outer electrons (including 2 of the other symbol); brackets and charges. (b) CaO (c) Strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; a giant ionic lattice with ions in a regular repeating arrangement.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct number of each ion; 1 mark: 8 electrons on anion with transferred electrons shown; 1 mark: charges [3] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark: electrostatic attraction; 1 mark: giant lattice [2]

items.stem: In an industrial process in Karachi, molten sodium chloride, NaCl, is electrolysed using inert electrodes. (a) Describe what is observed at each electrode. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. (c) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode. (d) Explain why graphite is used for the electrodes. (e) Describe the movement of electrons in the external circuit.
items.answer: (a) cathode: silvery liquid sodium forms; anode: bubbles of pale green gas (b) Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (c) 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (d) it conducts electricity and is inert (unreactive) with high melting point (e) from the anode through the wires to the cathode (via the power supply)

items.stem: Chloe is studying chlorine, proton number 17, mass number 35. (a) State the relative mass and relative charge of each type of sub-atomic particle. (b) Explain why the atom has no overall charge. (c) Chlorine forms the ion Cl⁻. Deduce the number of electrons in this ion and explain how it forms. (d) Another atom has 17 protons and 19 neutrons. State whether it is the same element and give its mass number.
items.answer: (a) proton: 1, +1; neutron: 1, 0; electron: 1/1836, −1 (b) It has equal numbers of protons (17) and electrons (17), so the charges cancel. (c) 18 electrons; the atom gains 1 electron(s). (d) Yes, same element (same proton number); mass number 36; it is an isotope.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each particle [3] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark: number; 1 mark: lose/gain [2] (d) 1 mark: same element; 1 mark: mass number [2]

items.stem: Ethan investigates the differences between nitric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration. (a) Write equations to show the dissociation of nitric acid and of ethanoic acid. (b) Predict which acid has the lower pH at the same concentration and explain why. (c) Write the ionic equation for the reaction of an acid with calcium carbonate.
items.answer: (a) HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻ (complete); CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (partial) (b) nitric acid: higher [H⁺] because fully dissociated (c) CaCO₃(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [2] (c) [2]

items.stem: Ethan weighs 2.00 g of copper(II) oxide, CuO, on a balance in a science fair project. (Ar: Cu = 64, O = 16) (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (a) Calculate the relative formula mass of CuO. (b) Calculate the number of formula units in the sample. (c) Calculate the mass of Cu in the sample. (d) Calculate the percentage by mass of Cu in CuO. (e) Calculate the mass of CuO that would contain twice as many particles as this sample.

Data for four substances: P: m.p. −114 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; Q: m.p. 660 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; R: m.p. 845 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes; S: m.p. 115 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no. Identify the metal and explain how the data support your answer. Describe the type of structure of each of the other substances.
items.answer: Q is the metal (conducts as solid and liquid – delocalised electrons). P: simple molecular; R: giant ionic; S: simple molecular
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal identified; 1 mark: conducts when solid due to delocalised electrons; 1 mark per two other structures correct up to [2] total [4]

items.stem: Sofia studies two reactions. Reaction 1: CuO(s) + Mg(s) → Cu(s) + MgO(s). Reaction 2: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). (a) Define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen. (b) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in reaction 1. (c) Write the two half-equations for reaction 2. (d) Identify the oxidising agent in reaction 2. (e) Explain why reaction 2 is a redox reaction even though no oxygen is involved.
items.answer: (a) oxidation: gain of oxygen; reduction: loss of oxygen (b) oxidised: magnesium; reduced: copper(II) oxide (c) Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (d) Cu²⁺ (e) electrons are transferred from Fe to Cu²⁺
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 1 mark each [2] (d) [1] (e) [1]

items.stem: Classify each change as physical or chemical: steam condensing on a window; sand being filtered from water; silver tarnishing; salt being separated from sea water by evaporation; bread being baked; magnesium burning in air.
items.answer: steam condensing on a window: physical; sand being filtered from water: physical; silver tarnishing: chemical; salt being separated from sea water by evaporation: physical; bread being baked: chemical; magnesium burning in air: chemical
items.markingKey: steam condensing on a window: physical; sand being filtered from water: physical; silver tarnishing: chemical; salt being separated from sea water by evaporation: physical; bread being baked: chemical; magnesium burning in air: chemical. 1 mark per two correct [3]

items.stem: Mohammed studies reaction X. The reactants have an energy of 370 kJ/mol, the products 145 kJ/mol and the transition state (top of the hump) 620 kJ/mol. (a) A catalyst reduces the activation energy by 140 kJ/mol. Describe the change to the diagram. (b) Explain why the catalyst increases the rate of reaction. (c) Calculate the activation energy of the reverse reaction.
items.answer: (a) peak lower by 140 kJ/mol (at 480 kJ/mol); reactant and product levels unchanged (b) lower Ea, so a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy ≥ Ea; more successful collisions per second (c) 475 kJ/mol

items.stem: Elena heats a sample of stearic acid until it melts, then records the temperature as it cools. Results: 0 min: 109 °C, 1 min: 101 °C, 2 min: 93 °C, 3 min: 85 °C, 4 min: 77 °C, 5 min: 69 °C, 6 min: 69 °C, 7 min: 69 °C, 8 min: 63 °C, 9 min: 57 °C, 10 min: 51 °C. (a) State the freezing point of the sample. (b) State the physical state(s) present at 0 min and at 6 min. (c) Describe how the movement of the particles changes during the first two minutes. (d) Calculate the rate of cooling, in °C/min, before freezing starts.
items.answer: (a) 69 °C (b) liquid; liquid and solid (c) Particles lose kinetic energy and move more slowly (still sliding past each other as a liquid). (d) 8 °C/min
items.markingKey: (a) temperature of the flat section [1] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) [1] (d) (109 − 101) ÷ 1 [1]

items.stem: Mateo heats 2.50 g of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O, in an evaporating basin until a white powder remains. Water is then added drop by drop to the cooled powder. (Ar: Cu = 64, H = 1, O = 16, S = 32) (a) Write the equation for the reversible reaction, including the ⇌ symbol. (b) Describe what is observed when the water is added. (c) State whether the forward reaction (heating) is endothermic or exothermic, giving a reason. (d) Suggest how cobalt(II) chloride could be used for the same purpose.
items.answer: (a) CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O (b) white powder turns blue; the mixture gets warm (c) endothermic: heat must be supplied to remove the water (d) blue anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride turns pink with water

items.stem: Mei investigates the reaction: zinc carbonate → zinc oxide + carbon dioxide. (a) Write the balanced symbol equation, including state symbols. (b) State the number of atoms of each element on the left-hand side. (c) Calculate the relative formula mass of ZnCO₃. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, Zn = 65) (d) Explain why the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. (e) Suggest why the mass of the reaction container may change if the reaction is done in an open beaker.
items.answer: (a) ZnCO₃(s) → ZnO(s) + CO₂(g) (b) C 1, O 3, Zn 1 (c) 125 (d) atoms are rearranged; none are created or destroyed (e) a gas is given off / taken in from the air
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark formulae; 1 mark balanced; 1 mark state symbols [3] (b) [1] (c) 65 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 125 [1] (d) [1] (e) [1]

items.stem: Daniel titrates 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide with sulfuric acid of unknown concentration, using methyl orange indicator. Titres (cm³): rough 32.00; titre 1: 31.25; titre 2: 31.25; titre 3: 31.25. 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre. Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm³.
items.answer: mean titre 31.25 cm³; concentration 0.0800 mol/dm³

items.stem: Boiling points of some simple molecular substances: ethane (C₂H₆): −89 °C, propane (C₃H₈): −42 °C, methane (CH₄): −162 °C. Describe the trend in boiling point with relative molecular mass and explain it.
items.answer: Boiling point increases as Mr increases (CH₄ 16, C₂H₆ 30, C₃H₈ 44): larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so more energy is needed to separate them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Mr values / ordering; 1 mark: b.p. increases with Mr; 1 mark: stronger intermolecular forces need more energy [3]

items.stem: Ines purifies copper by electrolysis. During the experiment the impure copper anode loses 6.40 g and the pure copper cathode gains 5.89 g. Calculate the percentage of copper in the impure anode and explain why the two masses are different.
items.answer: 92.0%; the anode also contained impurities, which fell as sludge or dissolved without being deposited.
items.markingKey: % = 5.89 ÷ 6.40 × 100 [1] = 92.0% [1]; impurities lost from anode do not deposit on cathode [1]

items.stem: Leila is given data for a sample of boron: mass 10: 19.9%; mass 11: 80.1%. (a) Calculate the relative atomic mass of the sample, to one decimal place. (b) The proton number of boron is 5. Give the number of neutrons in each isotope. (c) Another sample of boron from a different source has a slightly higher relative atomic mass. Suggest an explanation.
items.answer: (a) 10.8 (b) 10: 5, 11: 6 (c) It contains a higher proportion of the heavier isotope (11).

items.stem: Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of calcium oxide with hydrochloric acid, and state what this reaction shows about the type of oxide.
items.answer: CaO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l); calcium oxide is basic (it reacts with an acid)
items.markingKey: CaO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l): formulae [1]; balanced [1]; states [1]; type of oxide [1]

items.stem: Sofia is given a bottle labelled iron(II) sulfate and also studies the species FeO and H₂S. (a) Write the formula of the compound in the bottle. (b) State what the Roman numeral in the name tells you. (c) Deduce the oxidation number of Fe in FeO. (d) Deduce the oxidation number of S in H₂S. (e) State the rules you used to deduce oxidation numbers.
items.answer: (a) FeSO₄ (b) the oxidation number of the metal/element is +2 (c) 2 (d) -2 (e) elements 0; O −2; H +1; sum = 0 for compounds or = charge for ions

items.stem: A company in Madrid wants to make hydrogen faster from iron and hydrochloric acid. (a) State three changes that would increase the rate of reaction. (b) Describe how the rate could be measured. (c) Name the independent variable and two control variables for an investigation into the effect of temperature.
items.answer: (a) increase acid concentration; increase temperature; use smaller pieces / powder (or add a catalyst) (b) measure the volume of hydrogen produced at regular time intervals with a gas syringe (or mass loss on a balance) (c) independent: temperature; control: concentration and volume of acid, mass and size of iron
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) 1 mark apparatus; 1 mark timed readings [2] (c) 1 mark independent; 1 mark controls [2]

items.stem: State the sum of the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound.
items.answer: zero

items.stem: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process?
items.answer: vanadium(V) oxide
items.markingKey: V₂O₅ catalyses 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.

items.stem: Grace tests toothpaste and orange juice with universal indicator: they turn blue and orange respectively. Suggest the pH of each and explain what the colours show about the solutions.
items.answer: toothpaste: pH ≈ 9 (weakly alkaline); orange juice: pH ≈ 4 (weakly acidic). The lower pH solution has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: both pH values; 1 mark: classification; total [3]

items.stem: Samples of sulfur dioxide, SO₂, and neon, Ne, are released at the same time and temperature. Which statement is correct? (Ar: Ne = 20, O = 16, S = 32)
options: Neon diffuses faster because it has a lower Mr.
Both diffuse at the same rate because they are both gases.
Sulfur dioxide diffuses faster because it has a higher Mr.
Sulfur dioxide diffuses faster because it has a lower Mr.
items.answer: Neon diffuses faster because it has a lower Mr.
items.markingKey: Mr(SO₂) = 64, Mr(Ne) = 20: lower Mr → faster.

items.stem: For the reaction 2CH₃OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O, list the bonds broken and the bonds made, and explain how these determine whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: Broken: 6 × C–H, 2 × C–O, 2 × O–H, 3 × O=O. Made: 4 × C=O, 8 × O–H. If more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them, the reaction is exothermic; otherwise endothermic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: bonds broken; 1 mark: bonds made; 1 mark: comparison rule [4]

items.stem: Write the ionic half-equation for the formation of calcium at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten calcium chloride.
items.answer: Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ca
items.markingKey: Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ca: species [1]; electrons balanced [1]

items.stem: What is the proton number of an atom?
options: the number of protons in the nucleus
the number of neutrons in the nucleus
the number of electrons in the outer shell
the total number of particles in the atom
items.answer: the number of protons in the nucleus
items.markingKey: Proton number (atomic number) = number of protons; it identifies the element.

items.stem: On a graph of volume of gas against time, what does a steeper gradient show?
items.answer: a faster rate of reaction
items.markingKey: Gradient = rate.

items.stem: The melting point of magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, is 714 °C and that of sodium chloride, NaCl, is 801 °C. Explain why both melting points are high, and suggest why sodium chloride has the higher melting point.
items.answer: Both are giant ionic lattices with many strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions that need a lot of energy to overcome. Sodium chloride has smaller ions that are closer together (or more ions per unit), so the attraction is stronger.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: giant ionic lattice; 1 mark: strong electrostatic attraction needs much energy; 1 mark: comparison (charge / size of ions) [4]

items.stem: How many atoms in total are shown in the formula Ca(OH)₂?
Lucas says that 2 mol of oxygen gas occupies 24 dm³ at r.t.p. because oxygen is O₂. Explain the error and give the correct answer.
items.answer: Each mole of molecules occupies 24 dm³, so 2 mol occupies 48 dm³.

items.stem: Priya heats a sample of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, to constant mass. Mass of crucible = 18.95 g; crucible + hydrated salt = 25.20 g; crucible + anhydrous salt = 22.95 g. Calculate the value of x. (Ar: Cu = 64, H = 1, O = 16, S = 32)

Answer both parts. (a) Explain why adding more of the reactant that is in excess does not increase the mass of product. (b) A student obtains a percentage yield of 108% for a dried precipitate. Suggest a reason for this.
items.answer: (a) The amount of product depends on the limiting reactant; once it has all reacted, extra excess reactant has nothing to react with. (b) The product was not completely dry (still contained water) or was contaminated with another substance.

items.stem: Classify each of these as an element, a compound or a mixture: nitrogen, ammonia, air, bronze.
items.answer: nitrogen: element; ammonia: compound; air: mixture; bronze: mixture
items.markingKey: nitrogen: element; ammonia: compound; air: mixture; bronze: mixture. All 4 correct [2]; 3 or 2 correct [1] total [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why universal indicator is more useful than litmus for comparing two acids. (b) Explain the difference between a base and an alkali.
items.answer: (a) Universal indicator shows a range of colours corresponding to pH values, so it shows how acidic each solution is; litmus only shows acid or alkali. (b) A base is any substance that neutralises an acid (e.g. a metal oxide or hydroxide); an alkali is a base that dissolves in water.

items.stem: Sipho heats a sample of paraffin wax until it melts, then records the temperature as it cools. Results: 0 min: 86 °C, 1 min: 76 °C, 2 min: 66 °C, 3 min: 56 °C, 4 min: 56 °C, 5 min: 56 °C, 6 min: 52 °C, 7 min: 48 °C, 8 min: 44 °C, 9 min: 40 °C. (a) State the freezing point of the sample. (b) State the physical state(s) present at 0 min and at 4 min.
items.answer: (a) 56 °C (b) liquid; liquid and solid
items.markingKey: (a) temperature of the flat section [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A steel spoon is to be electroplated with silver. Name the anode, the cathode and a suitable electrolyte.
items.answer: anode: silver; cathode: steel spoon; electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why diamond is hard but graphite is soft, even though both contain only carbon atoms. (b) A student says, "Graphite has a low melting point because its layers slide easily." Explain the error.
items.answer: (a) In diamond each C is bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3D network of strong covalent bonds; graphite has layers held by weak forces that slide over each other. (b) Melting requires breaking the strong covalent bonds within the layers, so graphite has a very high melting point; the weak forces between layers only explain its softness.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: diamond rigid 3D 4 bonds; 1 mark: graphite layers with weak forces slide [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: In a water-testing laboratory, the rate of reaction of zinc with sulfuric acid is compared. experiment 1: small granules, 0.500 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C; experiment 2: small granules, 1.50 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C; experiment 3: powder, 1.50 mol/dm³ acid, 15 °C. Which experiment has the fastest initial rate?
items.answer: experiment 3
items.markingKey: Experiment 3 has conditions at least as favourable in every factor (concentration, temperature, surface area) and better in at least one.

items.stem: During a titration, Mohammed uses a measuring cylinder instead of a pipette for the alkali. Explain the effect on the results and how the procedure should be improved.
items.answer: A measuring cylinder is much less accurate, so the volume of alkali (and the calculated concentration) is less reliable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: effect; 1 mark: improvement [2]

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, how sodium sulfide forms when sodium reacts with sulfur. Include the electronic configurations of the atoms and ions (proton numbers: sodium 11, sulfur 16).
items.answer: Each sodium atom (2,8,1) loses 1 outer electron to form Na⁺ (2,8); each sulfur atom (2,8,6) gains 2 electrons to form S²⁻ (2,8,8). 2 sodium atoms transfer electrons to 1 sulfur atom, and the oppositely charged ions attract (ionic bond), giving Na₂S.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: sodium loses 1 electron(s); 1 mark: sulfur gains 2 electron(s); 1 mark: ions Na⁺ and S²⁻; 1 mark: configurations 2,8,1 → 2,8 and 2,8,6 → 2,8,8 [4]

items.stem: Chloe weighs 5.48 g of hydrogen chloride, HCl, on a balance in a college laboratory. (Ar: Cl = 35.5, H = 1) (Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol) (a) Calculate the relative formula mass of HCl. (b) Calculate the number of moles of H atoms in the sample. (c) Calculate the mass of H in the sample. (d) Calculate the percentage by mass of H in HCl. (e) Calculate the mass of HCl that would contain twice as many particles as this sample.

A technician in Lima needs formulae for three compounds: zinc sulfide, iron(II) chloride and silver sulfide. (a) Give the formula and charge of each ion present in the three compounds. (b) Calculate the relative formula mass of iron(II) chloride. (c) Explain why the formula of a compound containing a polyatomic ion sometimes needs brackets.
items.answer: (a) Zn²⁺, S²⁻; Fe²⁺, Cl⁻; Ag⁺, S²⁻ (b) 127 (c) to show that the subscript multiplies the whole group of atoms in the ion
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per compound [3] (b) 1 × 56 + 2 × 35.5 [2] (c) [1]

(c) Identify E. (d) Name another element with similar chemical properties to E and explain why. (e) Describe the arrangement of electrons in an atom of E in shells.
items.answer: (a) 2,4 (b) Group IV, Period 2: 4 outer electrons and 2 occupied shells. (c) carbon (d) any element in Group IV (same number of outer electrons) (e) shell 1: 2, shell 2: 4
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark: group; 1 mark: period; 1 mark: reasoning [3] (c) [1] (d) 1 mark: element; 1 mark: same number of outer electrons [2] (e) [1]

items.stem: Ana investigates two reactions in polystyrene cups. Reaction A: ethanol burns in a spirit burner; the temperature changes from 23 °C to 36 °C. Reaction B: ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate; the temperature changes from 23 °C to 17 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature change for each reaction. (b) Classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic, giving a reason. (c) State the sign of ΔH for each reaction. (d) Explain why a polystyrene cup is used rather than a glass beaker.
items.answer: (a) A: +13 °C; B: −6 °C (b) A exothermic (temperature rises); B endothermic (temperature falls) (c) A negative; B positive (d) polystyrene is a better insulator, reducing heat transfer with the surroundings
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: A cleaning company in Lima must choose between nitric acid and ethanoic acid (vinegar) for removing limescale (calcium carbonate). (a) Write equations to show the dissociation of nitric acid and of ethanoic acid. (b) Identify the proton donor and the proton acceptor in that reaction. (c) Evaluate which acid is better for the cleaning company.
items.answer: (a) HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻ (complete); CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (partial) (b) H⁺ (from the acid) donor; carbonate ion acceptor (c) strong acid works faster but is more corrosive/hazardous; ethanoic acid is safer for surfaces and users but slower – justified choice
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark each side; 1 mark conclusion [3]

items.stem: Noah places cotton wool soaked in concentrated aqueous ammonia at one end of a 80 cm glass tube and cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrobromic acid at the other end, then seals both ends. After a few minutes a white ring of ammonium bromide forms inside the tube. (a) Calculate the relative molecular masses of ammonia and hydrogen bromide. (b) State and explain which end of the tube the white ring forms nearer to. (c) The experiment is repeated with a 160 cm tube. Predict the effect on the time taken and on the relative position of the ring.
items.answer: (a) NH₃ = 17; HBr = 81 (b) Nearer the hydrogen bromide end, because ammonia has a lower Mr, so its molecules move faster and travel further in the same time. (c) Takes longer (further to travel); the ring still forms nearer the hydrogen bromide end at the same fraction of the length.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: nearer the hydrogen bromide end; 1 mark: lower Mr ammonia diffuses faster [2] (c) 1 mark: longer; 1 mark: same relative position [2]

items.stem: A technician in Madrid electrolyses aqueous sodium hydroxide with carbon electrodes and collects the products. (a) List all the ions present in the solution. (b) Name the product at the cathode and explain why it forms. (c) Name the product at the anode and explain why it forms. (d) Describe a test to identify the product at the anode. (e) Describe one change in the electrolyte during the experiment.
items.answer: (a) Na⁺, OH⁻, H⁺ (b) hydrogen: the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead (c) oxygen: there are no halide ions, so OH⁻ ions are discharged to give oxygen (d) a glowing splint relights (e) the concentration of the dissolved compound changes as ions are discharged
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark product; 1 mark reason [2] (c) 1 mark product; 1 mark reason [2] (d) [1] (e) [1]

items.stem: Data for four substances: P: m.p. 3550 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; Q: m.p. 660 °C, conducts as solid: yes, conducts when molten: yes; R: m.p. −114 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: no; S: m.p. 845 °C, conducts as solid: no, conducts when molten: yes. Identify the metal and explain how the data support your answer. Describe the type of structure of each of the other substances.
items.answer: Q is the metal (conducts as solid and liquid – delocalised electrons). P: giant covalent; R: simple molecular; S: giant ionic
items.markingKey: 1 mark: metal identified; 1 mark: conducts when solid due to delocalised electrons; 1 mark per two other structures correct up to [2] total [4]

items.stem: Freya reacts 0.120 g of magnesium ribbon with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (excess) at 25 °C. Volume of H₂: 0 s: 0 cm³, 20 s: 53 cm³, 40 s: 83 cm³, 60 s: 99 cm³, 80 s: 108 cm³, 100 s: 114 cm³, 120 s: 120 cm³, 140 s: 120 cm³. (Ar: Mg = 24) (a) Calculate the average rate over the first 40 s. (b) Describe the curve you would expect if 25 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ acid were used instead, with the same solid. (c) Describe the curve if half the mass of solid were used with the original acid.
items.answer: (a) 2.08 cm³/s (b) steeper at the start (more concentrated); same final volume (same amount of limiting solid) (c) slightly less steep at first; final volume halved (≈ 60.0 cm³)

items.stem: Kenji has two unlabelled solutions, P and Q. One is iron(II) sulfate solution and the other is acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Acidified potassium manganate(VII) and aqueous potassium iodide are available. (a) Describe the result expected when aqueous potassium iodide is added to the oxidising agent. (b) Explain the colour change with potassium iodide in terms of electrons. (c) State what happens to the oxidation number of manganese when manganate(VII) reacts with the reducing agent. (d) Suggest why the potassium manganate(VII) must be acidified.
items.answer: (a) colourless to brown (iodine formed) (b) the oxidising agent removes electrons from iodide ions: 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (c) decreases from +7 to +2 (reduced) (d) H⁺ ions are needed for the reduction of MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺

items.stem: Noah studies the dissociation of dinitrogen tetroxide (colourless) into nitrogen dioxide (brown): N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +58 kJ/mol. The reaction is carried out in a closed system. (a) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the yield. (b) Explain the effect of a catalyst on the rate and on the yield. (c) Explain why increasing the temperature increases the rate even if it lowers the yield. (d) Suggest why the system must be closed.
items.answer: (a) yield increases: the forward reaction is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to oppose the increase in temperature (b) rate increases (equilibrium reached sooner); yield unchanged (c) particles faster: more frequent, more energetic collisions (d) so that no reactants or products escape, allowing equilibrium to be established
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark effect; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [2] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.answer: Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s); spectator ions: Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻

items.stem: Freya adds an excess of magnesium to warm nitric acid to make crystals of magnesium nitrate. (a) Describe what is observed during the reaction. (b) Write the balanced symbol equation, with state symbols. (c) Explain why an excess of the solid is used.
items.answer: (a) fizzing as hydrogen is given off; the metal gets smaller (b) Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂ (c) to make sure all the acid reacts; excess removed by filtration

items.stem: Kwame traps argon in a gas syringe at constant pressure and measures its volume at different temperatures: 10 °C: 60.0 cm³, 35 °C: ? cm³, 60 °C: 70.6 cm³, 85 °C: 75.9 cm³, 110 °C: 81.2 cm³. (a) Explain the trend in terms of particles. (b) State one variable that must be kept constant and explain why. (c) Suggest why the syringe plunger must move freely.
items.answer: (a) Higher temperature → particles move faster → hit the plunger harder and more often → plunger pushed out until pressure balanced. (b) The pressure (or the amount/mass of gas, e.g. no leaks), because it also affects the volume. (c) So that the pressure inside stays equal to atmospheric pressure (constant pressure).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: faster particles; 1 mark: more / harder collisions push plunger out [2] (b) 1 mark: variable; 1 mark: reason [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: A city council in Jakarta is replacing petrol vans with hydrogen fuel cell vans. (a) Write the overall equation for the reaction in the fuel cell. (b) Name two pollutants produced by petrol engines that are not produced by fuel cells. (c) Evaluate whether the council has made a good decision.
items.answer: (a) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (b) carbon dioxide; carbon monoxide (also oxides of nitrogen, particulates) (c) balanced judgement: cleaner air and lower CO₂ vs cost, storage, refuelling infrastructure, source of hydrogen
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each [2] (c) 1 mark each side; 1 mark conclusion [3]

items.stem: A ceramics company in Nairobi uses potassium bromide, KBr (m.p. 734 °C), in its products. (a) Describe the structure of solid potassium bromide. (b) Describe and explain its electrical conductivity when solid and when molten. (c) Explain why the crystals are brittle. (d) Name the ions present and give the ratio in which they are present.
items.answer: (a) giant ionic lattice: regular 3D arrangement of alternating positive and negative ions (b) solid: does not conduct, ions fixed; molten: conducts, ions free to move (c) a force shifts layers so like-charged ions meet and repel, so the crystal cracks (d) K and Br ions in ratio 1:1
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: giant lattice; 1 mark: alternating oppositely charged ions [2] (b) 1 mark each state with reason [2] (c) [2] (d) [1]
